input:
Start-up
Before the first start of a shift, it is advisable to walk the pump and its lines and to satisfy yourself that everything is in order. You should confirm that the coupling guard is fitted and secure, that the suction and discharge lines are connected as the line-up sheet shows, and that no blanks or blinds remain in the line from maintenance. The lubricant in the bearing housing should be checked by the sight glass; if the level is low, it should be topped up with the specified oil, and the reason for the loss should ideally be found before the pump is run. Where a seal flush is fitted, the flush supply should be opened and flow confirmed at the seal drain. The pump must then be primed. The casing and the suction line are filled with the pumped liquid from the suction vessel, and the casing is vented at the vent point until liquid, rather than air, comes from the vent; it is important to understand that a centrifugal pump started dry or partly full of air does not develop head and runs its seals without liquid. The suction valve is opened fully. The discharge valve is set closed or nearly closed, as the pump's data sheet directs for starting. Where access allows, the shaft should be turned by hand to confirm that it rotates freely; a shaft that will not turn is reported, not forced. The motor is bumped once to check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing, with the coupling guard refitted immediately afterwards. The motor is then started. The discharge pressure gauge should be watched as the pump comes up to speed: pressure should rise promptly to the normal discharge band. The discharge valve is opened slowly and the pump brought onto line, with the flow and the suction pressure watched as the valve opens. As the pump settles, the seal should be checked: a small steady leakage at a packed seal is to be expected, while a mechanical seal should show no visible leakage. You should also listen for cavitation noise, a crackling sound like gravel passing through the casing; if it is heard, the pump should be stopped and the suction condition corrected before running on. Once the pump is steady, the discharge pressure, the flow, and the bearing condition are recorded in the log. The pump should be checked again after a short run at duty. A gland that drips steadily when cold may seal as it warms, and a flange that is dry at start-up may weep as the line reaches temperature; both are findings for the log either way, and neither should be left to be discovered by the next shift.

Normal operation
During normal running, the pump should be kept within its normal band of flow. Careful attention should be paid to the suction vessel level, because the suction condition depends on it: a falling level moves the pump towards cavitation, and the level is the earliest warning the operator gets. The discharge pressure and the flow should be read on each round and compared with the logged values from earlier rounds; a drift in either, at unchanged valve positions, is information about the pump or the line and should be reported, rather than compensated silently by moving valves. The bearing housings should be felt on each round, or their temperature indicators read where fitted; a housing that is warming round by round should be reported before it reaches the alarm. The seal condition should likewise be checked on each round: leakage that grows, or leakage that changes character, is reported the same day. Listening to the pump forms part of the round: new vibration, new noise, or a change in the sound of the flow is a finding. The pump must not be run against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve; at low flow the power the motor delivers turns to heat in the liquid trapped in the casing, and the temperature rises quickly. The suction valve must not be throttled to control flow; flow is controlled at the discharge side, because suction throttling starves the pump and invites cavitation. The pump and its surroundings should be kept clean and clear: a leak that is washed away without being reported removes the evidence the next round depends on. Where a standby pump is fitted on the same duty, a changeover to it should be made on the rota the site keeps, so that both machines are exercised and neither stands long enough to seize or to settle solids in its casing. The changeover is logged, and the pump taken off line is left primed and ready unless work on it is planned. Pressures, flow, and any change found are logged, with the time of the round.

Alarms
Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and no others are introduced in this chapter. The first alarm is low suction pressure. This alarm means that the pump is losing its suction condition: the vessel level is low, the suction line is obstructed, or the liquid is vaporising at the eye of the impeller. On this alarm, the pump should be stopped. The suction vessel level and the suction line are checked, any obstruction found is cleared, the casing is vented, and the pump is reprimed before any restart is attempted. The pump should not be restarted against the alarm in the hope that the condition clears; a pump run in cavitation damages its impeller and its seals, and the damage is done while the condition lasts. The second alarm is high bearing temperature. This alarm means that the bearing is running hotter than its design allows, most often from low or degraded lubricant, misalignment, or a load the bearing is beginning to fail under. On this alarm, the pump should be stopped and the bearing allowed to cool. The lubricant level and its condition are checked, and the cause is looked for before restart; a bearing that has alarmed once and is restarted without a cause found will alarm again, with less margin. Both alarms should be reported in the log with the action taken, whether or not the pump is returned to service. An alarm that recurs after the action has been taken should be treated as a defect report, not a running instruction: the pump is withdrawn, the defect is raised for maintenance, and the alarm history from the log goes with the report.

Shutdown
For a stop to standby, the motor is stopped, the discharge valve is closed, and the pump is left primed and full, ready to start, with the suction valve open. For a planned stop, the flow is first reduced by closing the discharge valve towards the minimum the data sheet allows, and the motor is then stopped. The discharge valve is closed fully, followed by the suction valve. If the pump is to stand idle for a long period, or is to be opened, the casing should be drained through the drain point and vented, so that no liquid is trapped against the seals and no pressure remains in the casing. A pump standing full of a liquid that can crystallise, set, or corrode is drained and flushed before it is left. Where the liquid is hot, the pump should be allowed to cool before it is drained, and drained to the closed drain system, not to the floor. Where the liquid is hazardous, the draining and venting are done under the site permit arrangements, with the same proof of isolation before any joint is broken. The pump must be isolated electrically before any work is done on it, and the isolation locked and tagged; the lock is removed only by the person who fitted it, on completion of the work. Before any joint on the pump is broken, it must be proved that the casing is drained and vented: a joint slackened against trapped pressure or trapped liquid releases both at the fitter. The pump is left in the state the next shift needs, and the stop, the reason for it, and the state the pump was left in are recorded.
